Executive Summary

What the business is

NVIDIA sells connected computing platforms—GPUs, networking, systems and software—to cloud providers, server makers and businesses. A GPU is a processor that handles many tasks at once; a cloud provider rents computing power and storage over the internet. Fiscal 2026 revenue was $215,938 million, led by Data Center.

How do you analyze a stock with Claude?

Before the first question, attach the right reports and paste the rules. Companies must send their regulator a set of reports, called filings: find them on the company’s investor-relations page, or on EDGAR, the US database (SEDAR+ in Canada).

Step 1. Attach what each question needs

  • the last three annual reports (10-Ks in the US) and the latest quarterly report (a 10-Q);
  • the last eight earnings releases and call transcripts;
  • the proxy statement, and the list of insider filings (Form 4s) as text.

Step 2. Paste the rules first

  • paste the rules below before the first question;
  • they ask for the document, page, sentence, period, unit and currency of every number;
  • save them in a Claude Project and every new chat in it starts with them.

The rules: “You are an equity research analyst, and you use only the documents I attached. For every number, give the document, the page, the exact sentence, the period, the unit and the currency. If the documents do not answer, write “not in the documents”, and never tell me to buy or sell it.”

Claude takes up to 20 files a chat, its help page says, so ask the first four questions in one chat and the last four in a fresh one.

Which Claude prompts work for stock analysis?

Eight prompts, one for each chapter of a full report. Paste them one at a time, swap in the company’s name for [company], and read each answer before the next.

  • 1. The business: how it makes money

    “Explain how [company] makes money, in plain words. List each product line, who pays for it and its share of revenue last year. Name any customer above 10% of revenue.”

  • 2. The market: who else is in the room

    “Describe the market [company] sells into: its size, whether it is growing, and its three to five closest rivals. What protects [company] from them? List the biggest risks, including any dependence on one country, customer or product.”

  • 3. History: where the cash went

    “Tell me how [company] got here. List its five biggest decisions of the last five years: acquisitions, big investments, dividends, share buybacks and debt. Then show where the cash went in each of those years.”

  • 4. Management: who runs it, who owns it

    “List the executives and directors: time in the role, previous jobs, pay and what their bonus depends on. Who owns the biggest stakes? Then, from the Form 4 list I paste in, split the last 12 months of insider trades into market trades, stock awards, tax withholding and gifts.”

  • 5. The numbers: years and quarters

    “Give me five fiscal years and the last eight quarters of revenue, operating profit, net profit, earnings per share, cash from operations, capital spending and free cash flow. Then subtract stock pay from free cash flow and show the result.”

  • 6. Valuation: what you pay

    “The share price is $[price]. What do investors pay for [company]? Give the price-to-earnings ratio on the last 12 months and the next 12, the free cash flow yield and the enterprise value, showing each sum.”

  • 7. What comes next: the promises

    “What has management guided for the next quarter and the next year, with its date? For each of the last eight quarters, did the result land above, within or below the guided range? List the biggest planned spending and say whether cash from operations can pay for it.”

  • 8. Where the price could go

    “Build bear, base and bull cases for the share price in one, two and three years. Give each one’s revenue, profit margin, share count, multiple and chance, adding up to 100%. Say what would change each case, and do not tell me to buy or sell.”

Where does Claude get a stock wrong, and how do you check it?

Claude is only as right as the pages in front of it, so make every answer point to its page. Five checks do that: three you do, two you paste.

  • 1. Find the sentenceSearch the filing for the exact number, and drop it if it is not there.
  • 2. Check the period, the unit and the currencyTSMC reports in New Taiwan dollars and its US shares trade in US dollars, so a ratio that mixes them is wrong.
  • 3. Redo the sumAsk Claude to show its arithmetic, and redo it.
  • 4. Paste at the end“Now argue against your own conclusion, using only the documents.”
  • 5. Paste after every answer“What is the date of the newest document you used, and which results has it not seen?”

Executive Summary

What the business is

NVIDIA sells connected computing platforms—GPUs, networking, systems and software—to cloud providers, server makers and businesses. A GPU is a processor that handles many tasks at once; a cloud provider rents computing power and storage over the internet. Fiscal 2026 revenue was $215,938 million, led by Data Center. A dollar comes in when a direct customer buys a platform or software, while a cloud provider may rent its resulting capacity to an AI company or business. Software may be licensed, subscribed to or included with hardware.

  • Concentration: Data Center produced $193,737 million in fiscal 2026, versus $16,042 million from Gaming and $2,349 million from Automotive.
  • Platform economics: A sale can bundle GPUs, networking and CUDA, NVIDIA’s software tools for programming GPUs. NVIDIA does not disclose separate software revenue or renewal rates.
  • Outsourced production: NVIDIA designs products but relies on specialists for fabrication, packaging, memory, testing and assembly. Supply and capacity commitments reached $279 billion at July 2026.
  • Cash timing: Sales can precede cash. Days sales outstanding reached 60 days, and five direct customers represented 70% of accounts receivable at July 2026.

The challenges

  • Customer payback: Cloud providers must recover equipment, networking, power, cooling, staff and financing costs through paid workloads or savings. Low utilization or weak returns could pause the next spending cycle.
  • Platform substitution: CUDA familiarity can make switching costly, but customers may port workloads to AMD ROCm or custom chips. The risk is greatest if alternatives deliver better economics on real workloads.
  • System delivery and supply: A platform needs processors, memory, networking, assembly, power and cooling to arrive together. NVIDIA’s $279 billion of commitments increases the cost of a demand or product mismatch.
  • Export restrictions: Policy can block sales after inventory and supplier commitments are in place. NVIDIA recorded a $4.5 billion H20 charge after U.S. export restrictions.
